title: Watchful Mama Bear Gemini Wins the Helicopter Mom Award
summary:
Even bears can be helicopter parents. The term, coined in the 1990s by child development researchers Foster Cline and Jim Fay, describes overly cautious parents who constantly monitor, control, and hover over their children's activities out of fear.

For these watchful tendencies, the U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska has awarded a brown bear named Gemini with the 2026 Helicopter Mom Award.

"We understand her choice, weighing the dangers of being around other bears at a prime fishing location," the rangers write. "Still, we hope we see a lot more of them next year."

Gemini kept an eye on her cubs around other bears fishing in Alaska's Anan Creek. The numbers also back up Gemini and other mother bears' watchfulness. Brown bear cubs in Alaska have a roughly 50 percent survival rate within their first year, while the black bear cub survival rate can range from 51 to 88 percent depending on the location. Gemini has also had cubs in 2023 and 2024.

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory over the summer.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears. Like their counterparts further north in Katmai National Park, the bears return annually each summer to eat salmon and teach their young how to fish and survive. Every bear here exhibits their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear, while explore.org's cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.
why_it_matters: Gemini's story shows why mother animals stay close to their young in the wild, and how rangers learn about bears by watching them summer after summer.

background_read: A helicopter parent is a parent who watches and controls their children very closely, often because they worry about danger.
Mother bears must protect cubs that are small and vulnerable, especially around other bears at busy fishing spots.
Salmon runs bring many bears to the same creek each summer, giving rangers a chance to watch and name individual bears.
Awards like the Anan Bear Awards are a fun way for rangers to share what they learn about each bear's habits.
